passage:
Since 1993, satellite altimeters have produced a continuous record of global mean sea level. Researchers maintaining the dataset argue that it shows more than a simple rise: the rate of rise has itself increased over time. A student preparing a public talk wants to use the decadal averages below to argue that the satellite record demonstrates an accelerating rate of sea-level rise across the past three decades rather than a constant rate, because _______

Mean rate of global mean sea-level rise by decadal window (satellite altimetry)
| Decadal window | Mean rate of rise (mm per year) |
|---|---|
| 1993-2002 | 2.7 |
| 1998-2007 | 3.1 |
| 2003-2012 | 3.0 |
| 2008-2017 | 3.8 |
| 2013-2022 | 4.5 |
question: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support the claim?

choices.text: the 1998-2007 rate (3.1 mm per year) was slightly higher than the 2003-2012 rate (3.0 mm per year).
the mean rate of rise climbed from 2.7 mm per year in 1993-2002 to 4.5 mm per year in 2013-2022, the latest window showing the fastest rate.
the cumulative rise across the full record reached roughly 100 mm, the largest total the satellite record has documented.
the 2008-2017 rate (3.8 mm per year) falls between the earliest and latest windows, showing that the rate has held essentially steady.

explanation: The correct answer is B. To show acceleration, the data must trace the rate climbing across the record, ending at its highest value, and B does that by moving from the earliest window's 2.7 mm per year to the latest window's 4.5 mm per year. A cites a one-tenth difference between two middle windows, far too small to establish a trend; C reports a cumulative total, which speaks to how much the sea has risen but not to whether the rate is changing; and D actually argues for a steady rate, the opposite of the claim.
